To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) eyewitnesses are more likely to make false identifications when they are asked to identify the culprit from a lineup or photospread that includes a foil who looks like the culprit, (b) eyewitnesses are also more likely to make such false identifications when the foil is selected on the basis of a verbal description of the culprit that the eyewitness provided, (c) eyewitnesses are less likely to make a false identification when the lineup or photospreads is conducted in double-blind fashion,

eyewitnesses should not be told that a lineup or photospread contains the culprit, that lineup administrators should select distractors that are most similar to the eyewitness’s description of the perpetrator (and not just to the perpetrator), and that the confidence with which eyewitnesses identify a suspect should be assessed and documented at the time of the lineup or photospreads.

the use of double-blind lineup testing, the use of a verbal description of the culprit, and the assessment of eyewitness confidence are recommended as procedures that can reduce the risk that an innocent person will be misidentified by an eyewitness.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the best way to conduct a lineup is one where the eyewitness does not know the suspect is present, the eyewitness has a description of the perpetrator that is used to select the distractors, and the person conducting the lineup does not know who the suspect is.
